passages.t: Imitate God and walk in love; no immorality, impurity or greed
passages.happening:
Chapter 4 ended with forgiveness. Chapter 5 goes on: “Be imitators of God, therefore, as beloved children, and walk in love, just as Christ loved us and gave Himself up for us as a fragrant sacrificial offering to God” (verses 1-2).

Then Paul names what love leaves behind. “But among you, as is proper among the saints, there must not be even a hint of sexual immorality, or of any kind of impurity, or of greed” (verse 3). Nor “obscenity, foolish talk, or crude joking”, “but rather thanksgiving” (verse 4).

He gives a warning: “No immoral, impure, or greedy person (that is, an idolater), has any inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God” (verse 5). “Let no one deceive you with empty words, for because of such things the wrath of God is coming on the sons of disobedience. Therefore do not be partakers with them” (verses 6-7).
passages.hearers:
Children copy their parents. They pick up the way a father talks and the way a mother laughs. Paul says believers are God's ‘beloved children’, so they are to copy him. And he shows exactly what that looks like: love that gives itself away, as Christ did on the cross.

‘A fragrant sacrificial offering’ is the language of Israel's altar. When a sacrifice was burned, its smoke rose to God as ‘a pleasing aroma’. Paul says Christ's death was that kind of offering. His self-giving love was the gift that pleased God most.

Then comes the contrast. In the cities the readers knew, sexual licence was widely tolerated, especially for men, and so was cheating in business. Paul says believers will be different, not by a little but altogether: ‘not even a hint’.

Notice that greed sits right beside sexual sin, and Paul calls the greedy person ‘an idolater’. Greed treats money or things as if they were God, the thing you trust to make you safe and happy. He says the same in Colossians: “greed, which is idolatry” (Colossians 3:5).

And notice what Paul puts in place of crude joking. Not grim silence, but ‘thanksgiving’. A grateful heart is the opposite of a grasping one.
passages.ot:
God told Israel, “be holy, because I am holy” (Leviticus 11:44). Paul's ‘be imitators of God’ says the same thing as a family likeness: children look like their Father.

The ‘fragrant’ offering goes back to Israel's sacrifices: the burnt offering was “a pleasing aroma, an offering made by fire to the LORD” (Exodus 29:18). Even after the flood, the first sacrifice is called a pleasing aroma to God (Genesis 8:21).

And the link between greed and idolatry is already in the Ten Commandments, which begin with “You shall have no other gods before Me” (Exodus 20:3) and end with “You shall not covet” (Exodus 20:17). The first and last commandments meet in the greedy heart.
passages.hard:
Verse 5 says that no immoral, impure or greedy person ‘has any inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God’. Who is Paul speaking about, and is this meant to frighten believers?

First, look at the list. Paul puts greed beside sexual sin. No honest reader can treat this as a list of other people's sins; most of us know greed from the inside. Churches have sometimes been loud about some sins on this list and quiet about others, and that is not how Paul reads.

Second, look at who he is speaking to. He is not shouting at the city outside. He is warning believers not to drift back into a way of life they had left, and not to be fooled by ‘empty words’ that say it does not matter. Many readers take verse 5 to describe a life settled in these things without turning back, not a believer who falls and repents. After a similar list Paul writes, “And that is what some of you were. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified, in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God” (1 Corinthians 6:11). Christians differ on whether a true believer can finally fall away. These notes do not choose. The note on Romans 8:31-39 and the Honest Answer ‘Can you lose your salvation?’ set out the views.

Third, these words give no one leave for contempt. Every person, on this list or off it, is someone God made and Christ died for. The warning is spoken so that people turn and live.

If you are a person whose conscience never rests, who keeps checking whether you have really believed, hear John's words: “Even if our hearts condemn us, God is greater than our hearts, and He knows all things” (1 John 3:20). Such fear can be part of anxiety or a habit of the mind, and that is not a failure of faith. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust, and if the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor or a doctor can help too. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Paul says the way to be like God is to love as Christ loved, by giving yourself away. Ask where your love has stayed comfortable and cost you nothing. Ask which sin on Paul's list you are most likely to excuse in yourself while noticing it in others. And ask what place thanksgiving has in the way you speak.

passages.happening:
Paul reminds the readers who they are. “For you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. Walk as children of light” (verse 8), “for the fruit of the light consists in all goodness, righteousness, and truth” (verse 9).

So they are to “Test and prove what pleases the Lord” (verse 10), and to have nothing to do with “the fruitless deeds of darkness, but rather expose them” (verse 11). Some things are too shameful even to talk about (verse 12). “But everything exposed by the light becomes visible, for everything that is illuminated becomes a light itself” (verse 13).

Then he quotes a saying: “Wake up, O sleeper, rise up from the dead, and Christ will shine on you” (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
Notice exactly what Paul says. Not ‘you were in the dark’, but ‘you were darkness’. And not ‘you are in the light now’, but ‘you are light in the Lord’. Becoming a Christian is not just moving to a new room. It is becoming a new kind of person.

The ‘fruit of the light’ is goodness, righteousness and truth. Fruit is not forced. It grows when the plant is healthy. Light, given time, produces a good life.

‘Test and prove what pleases the Lord’ means that believers have to think. Not every choice comes with a rule attached. They are to weigh things and learn, over time, what pleases God.

What does ‘expose’ mean? It is not a call to hunt for other people's sins. It means bringing what is hidden into the light, where it can be seen for what it is and healed. Light does two things: it shows what is wrong, and it changes what it touches. Verse 13 even says that what is lit up ‘becomes a light itself’.

The saying in verse 14 is not from the Old Testament, and no one knows its exact source. Many readers think it comes from an early Christian hymn, perhaps sung when new believers were baptized. It is a call to a sleeper to wake up, to someone dead to rise. That is what had happened to the readers (2:1-5).
passages.ot:
The light that comes to people in darkness is an old promise. “The people walking in darkness have seen a great light; on those living in the land of the shadow of death, a light has dawned” (Isaiah 9:2).

The saying in verse 14 sounds like Isaiah's call to Jerusalem, “Arise, shine, for your light has come, and the glory of the LORD rises upon you” (Isaiah 60:1), and his promise about the dead: “Your dead will live; their bodies will rise. Awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust” (Isaiah 26:19).

The Psalms say that all real light comes from God: “For with You is the fountain of life; in Your light we see light” (Psalm 36:9). And Proverbs pictures a good life as dawn growing brighter: “The path of the righteous is like the first gleam of dawn, shining brighter and brighter until midday” (Proverbs 4:18).
passages.asks: Paul says you are light, not only that you have light. Ask what part of your life you have kept in the dark, away from God and from the people who love you. Ask whether you are quicker to expose other people's wrongs than your own. And hear the call of verse 14 as spoken to you: wake up.

passages.t: Walk wisely: not drunk with wine, but filled with the Spirit
passages.happening:
“Pay careful attention, then, to how you walk, not as unwise but as wise, redeeming the time, because the days are evil” (verses 15-16). “Therefore do not be foolish, but understand what the Lord’s will is” (verse 17).

Then a contrast: “Do not get drunk on wine, which leads to reckless indiscretion. Instead, be filled with the Spirit” (verse 18).

Paul shows what that filling looks like: “Speak to one another with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs. Sing and make music in your hearts to the Lord, always giving thanks to God the Father for everything in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ” (verses 19-20).
passages.hearers:
‘Redeeming the time’ uses a word from the market: buying something up. Paul means making the most of each chance to do good, the way a shopper snaps up a bargain, because the days are hard and the chances will not last.

In Ephesus, feasts and drinking parties were part of public life, and so was the worship of Dionysus, the god of wine. People drank to forget, to feel bold, to lose themselves. Paul sets two kinds of filling side by side. Wine, taken to excess, leads to ‘reckless indiscretion’, a life that loses control and wastes itself. The Spirit leads somewhere else entirely.

Notice what the Spirit's filling looks like. Not wild feelings, but people singing together, giving thanks, and (as the next verse says) submitting to one another. In Greek verses 18 to 21 are one long sentence: be filled with the Spirit, speaking, singing, giving thanks, submitting. The Spirit's filling shows up in how a church sounds and how its people treat one another.

‘Psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs’ probably means all kinds of worship song, old and new. And notice that the songs are sung ‘to one another’ as well as to the Lord. Singing together teaches and strengthens the whole church.
passages.ot:
Proverbs warns again and again about too much wine: “Wine is a mocker, strong drink is a brawler, and whoever is led astray by them is not wise” (Proverbs 20:1). “Do not join those who drink too much wine or gorge themselves on meat” (Proverbs 23:20).

Yet the Psalms also count wine among God's good gifts: “wine that gladdens the heart of man, oil that makes his face to shine, and bread that sustains his heart” (Psalm 104:15).

The call to use time wisely is the prayer of Psalm 90: “So teach us to number our days, that we may present a heart of wisdom” (Psalm 90:12). And Israel's worship was full of thanks and song: “Let us enter His presence with thanksgiving; let us make a joyful noise to Him in song” (Psalm 95:2).
passages.hard:
Does verse 18 mean Christians must never drink? Christians agree that drunkenness is sin, that no one should be pressured to drink, that people harmed by alcohol and people caught in it need care, and that believers should not despise one another over a matter Scripture leaves to conscience (Romans 14). Beyond that they differ, and these notes do not choose.

Many Baptist, Methodist, Holiness and Pentecostal churches have long taught or encouraged abstaining from alcohol altogether. They point to its power to harm and enslave, the warnings of Proverbs, and the call in Romans 14 to give up a freedom for the sake of others.

Many other Christians, among them Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Anglican and Reformed churches, hold that drinking in moderation is a lawful use of God's gift. They point to Psalm 104, the wedding at Cana and wine at the Lord's Supper, while warning just as seriously against drunkenness.

Both take the danger seriously, and both honour the gift of a clear mind. Paul's own point is about what fills you and what you hand yourself over to.

If drinking has become hard to control, you do not have to face it alone. Tell someone you trust, and reach out to a doctor or a recovery group near you. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Ask what you reach for when you want to feel bold, calm or free: a drink, a screen, a purchase, or God. Ask whether your days show the Spirit's filling, in song, in thanks and in the way you treat people. And ask what one chance to do good this week you need to ‘buy up’ before it is gone.

passages.t: Submit to one another: wives and husbands, Christ and the church
passages.happening:
Paul opens with a word for every believer: “Submit to one another out of reverence for Christ” (verse 21).

Then he speaks to wives. “Wives, submit to your husbands as to the Lord. For the husband is the head of the wife as Christ is the head of the church, His body, of which He is the Savior. Now as the church submits to Christ, so also wives should submit to their husbands in everything” (verses 22-24).

Then, at greater length, to husbands. “Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ loved the church and gave Himself up for her” (verse 25), to make her holy and glorious (verses 26-27). “In the same way, husbands ought to love their wives as their own bodies. He who loves his wife loves himself” (verse 28). No one hates his own body, “but he nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ does the church” (verse 29).

Paul quotes Genesis: “For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife, and the two will become one flesh” (verse 31). “This mystery is profound, but I am speaking about Christ and the church” (verse 32). He ends: “each one of you also must love his wife as he loves himself, and the wife must respect her husband” (verse 33).
passages.hearers:
Verse 21 is the hinge. It ends the long sentence about being filled with the Spirit, and it opens the household passage. In some of the earliest Greek copies verse 22 has no verb of its own. It reads, in effect, ‘wives, to your husbands’, borrowing ‘submit’ from verse 21. So what Paul asks of wives grows out of what he asks of everyone.

The first hearers lived in Roman households. By law the father of the house held great power over his wife, his children and his slaves. Writers on running a household spoke to the man about how to rule the others. Paul does something different. He speaks to wives directly, as people who answer to Christ for themselves. And he gives husbands not rights but a cross: love her as Christ loved the church and ‘gave Himself up for her’. Roman custom put up with husbands who used slaves and prostitutes. Paul tells a husband to love his wife as his own body.

The ‘washing with water’ (verse 26) may echo the bath a bride took before her wedding. Many readers also hear baptism.

Much is agreed by Christians who read the rest of this passage differently. Marriage pictures Christ's love for the church. The husband's love is to be costly and self-giving, measured by the cross. Paul never tells a husband to make his wife submit. He speaks that word to wives themselves, so ‘submit’ is never a husband's to demand or enforce. Husband and wife stand before Christ as equal members of his body. And nothing here gives anyone a licence to control, frighten or harm another person.
passages.ot:
Paul quotes Genesis 2:24, God's word at the first marriage. The BSB of Genesis has “and they will become one flesh”. Paul has ‘the two’, as Jesus did when he quoted the verse (Matthew 19:5).

The prophets had already called God Israel's husband. “For your husband is your Maker” (Isaiah 54:5). “So I will betroth you to Me forever; I will betroth you in righteousness and justice, in loving devotion and compassion” (Hosea 2:19). In Ezekiel, God finds Israel abandoned, makes a covenant with her, and says, “Then I bathed you with water, rinsed off your blood, and anointed you with oil” (Ezekiel 16:9). Paul's picture of Christ washing and adorning his bride stands in that line.

And Malachi calls a wife “your companion and your wife by covenant” (Malachi 2:14). Marriage in Scripture is a covenant of faithfulness, not a contract of ownership.
passages.hard:
Christians agree on much here, as ‘What the first hearers would catch’ sets out above. They differ on what ‘head’ and ‘submit’ ask of a marriage today. These notes do not choose. The site's chapter note on Ephesians 5 sets out both readings; here they are in short, each as its own holders would put it.

Complementarians hold that men and women are equal in dignity and worth but given different callings in marriage. They read ‘head’ mainly as one who leads and bears responsibility, as Christ leads the church. They read verse 21 as the heading over what follows, with each person yielding in the way that fits the relationship, and a wife's submission as a gift she freely gives, never something taken. They note that Paul grounds the pattern in Christ and the church and in Genesis 2, not in Roman custom, so they believe it is meant to last. And they insist that the husband's calling, to die to himself, is the heavier one, and that headship never licenses harshness or control.

Egalitarians hold that men and women are equal in dignity and in calling. They read verse 21, ‘Submit to one another’, as governing the whole passage, so that husband and wife yield to each other. Many read ‘head’ as the one who gives life and nourishes, as Christ ‘nourishes and cherishes’ the church (verse 29), or as source. They see Paul working inside the household of his day while changing it from within, as with slavery in 6:5-9, and they believe the direction of the gospel (Galatians 3:28) points to marriages of mutual submission.

Both are held by Christians who honour Scripture. It is a question that divides faithful churches, not the faith.

Nothing in this passage asks anyone to stay where they or their children are in danger. If you are in an abusive marriage, seek safety first. Talk to a pastor or a counselor you trust, or call a local domestic violence line. These notes are not legal advice.

If you are being hurt in some other place, at home, at work or in a church, the same is true. Tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Verse 21 speaks to everyone before it speaks to anyone. Ask where you insist on your own way. If you are a husband, ask whether your love looks more like Christ's cross or like a claim to be served. If you are a wife, ask what it means to honour Christ in your marriage. And whoever you are, ask whether your home is a place where everyone is safe.
